lectures.title: Job Listing and Foregrounding: The `jobs` and `fg` Commands

cues.en: Let's now have a more in-depth look at the job management in Bash.
So let's say we started a job that is now running in the background.
How can we list all of the jobs that are running in the background?
Because maybe we are not just running one job in the background, but we want to run multiple jobs at
the same time in the background.
How can we have an overview over that?
So when Ping is running in the background, the way to list all the background jobs is with the jobs
command so we can just enter jobs and this will print all the jobs that are currently running.
So I would say let's just have a look at this.
So let's say here I'm running the ping command and I do want to redirect the output, but I don't want
to redirect it into a file because I'm really not interested in the output so I can redirect it into
a virtual file.
The file slash dev null, which if we write to it, it will just be discarded.
If we would read from it, we would just read zeros.
Um, so here I just redirect it into okay, let's throw back and let's throw away our output and I want
to run this in the background.
So now we can see that this job has been started in the background and it's running there.
Now, if I want to list the currently running jobs, that was our jobs command and we can see that this
job here right now, this one here is running.
The nice thing about this is that I could also, for example, just do another ping to another server.
Let's say, for example, Bing.com.
And I also redirect the output to because I'm not interested in it and this is now also running in the
background.
And if I now output all the jobs, you can see that two tasks are running in the background.
This is the first ping command, this is the second ping command.
And of course it wouldn't need to be just a ping command.
I could use any command that I could come up with for bash here.
I'm just using Ping because I don't want anything that takes a lot of my processing power.
So I don't want the CPU intensive task.
I don't want anything that uses a lot of network bandwidth.
So I'm just using the ping command here as a placeholder for any other possible command that I could
come up with.
So we can see that those two jobs are now running in the background and I'm able to use my shell at
the same time to do something else.
But let's say I want to switch to one of those jobs and I want to see what's actually happening there.
And for this, I can use the foreground command, which brings a background job back to foreground.
So if we have a job and we want to bring it to foreground, we can use this command.
And the way to go is that we could supply or that we could pass in a percentage with the job ID to bring
this job back to foreground.
So, for example, this one would bring the first job back to foreground.
If there's just one job, it will automatically switch to that and we don't need to specify the job
ID, We could just say foreground if there are multiple jobs, it will switch to the current job, which
is marked with a plus.
But don't worry about it too much.
We'll have a look at this in the terminal in a second.
So let's switch over to our terminal so we can see here those jobs, those jobs here.
No, they are done now because I've recorded the slides, so I need to restart those jobs.
So I hit clear.
And now, for example, this one here will this one will be our first job.
And this one here to the pink to Google.com.
That will be our second job.
So if I now list the job, you can see that those two jobs here are running.
Let's say I want to switch to a job now because right now they're still running in the background.
And you can see here, this is this job is indicated with this plus symbol.
So this means if I now just use the foreground command, I will by default switch to that job and yours,
we can see here, this is the job that's running.
And we are now as if we had typed that job into the terminal ourselves without putting it into the background.
So if I now, for example, would enter anything here, it will be sent to the ping program.
And the ping program usually throws away the standard input or doesn't listen to it.
So nothing happens here.
One thing we could do here right now would be, for example, to send a signal to that process.
For example, for now I would send the control C signal for the interrupt.
So I would send the interrupt signal and now my job has been cancelled.
So I would if I now list the jobs again, you can see here how I've switched to that job and how I canceled
that job.
So let me just copy that one here and start that job again.
So I clear my screen again because I want to show you something else.
So we have those two jobs that are running.
And let's say I want to switch to the first job.
Then I could say foreground and I could say I would like to switch to the job with.
Job ID one so I could just use this command.
And now you can see here how this.
Yeah, how I've switched to that job and actually it has completed within a few seconds because it was
already running for a few minutes.
So it's yeah, that's why I'm back in my batch.
But otherwise the ping program would still be active and user input would no longer work.
But because the program now has finished, we can see this here.
Only the second job is still running.
That's why it worked like this.
We can see there's still the second job that's still running and this is now marked with a plus.
So I could say either foreground or to use the percentage way to write it, I could say I want to switch
to this job.
And now I'm here at this job and I can now, for example, also send an interrupt again, Control C
and now this job has been quit or canceled or interrupted and it has come to an end.
So this is how this job management works.
There's one thing I want to emphasize because I feel like I pretty much showed you the effect, but
I feel like I should clarify it on the slide one more time.
So when we are using jobs in bash, only foreground jobs can receive keyboard input.
So whenever a job is running in the background.
So for example here, if I would, for example, start something here in the background, whatever I
do here in the terminal, it will still be it will still be parsed and it will still just reach the
terminal.
It will never reach our ping command because that's running in the background.
Also, for example, if I would send an interrupt here, it wouldn't interrupt anything because the
ping program is running in the background and it does it's not connected to my keyboard input that I'm
doing here in my shell.
So what I want to emphasize is that only foreground jobs can receive keyboard input and that also includes
signals.
For example, Sigint.
They will only work for foreground jobs and will only be parsed by those.
So background jobs never receive keyboard input.
You need to connect your terminal to those with the foreground command first and then those jobs can
receive keyboard input.
But as long as they are in the background, they are not able to receive keyboard input.
It's completely disconnected.
So this is already one part of the process or job management that we can do in batch, that we can start
something in the background and then that we can put it back to foreground that program.
But we can also start something and then tell Bash, Hey, we want to send this program to the background
and we will have a look at this in the next lecture, how this works.
